title: Real Arbitrage-Bot Wins: Documented Cases, Mechanics, and What a Small Bot Can Actually Exploit
summary: Documented crypto arbitrage falls into two honest buckets. (1) The legendary headline wins — SBF/Alameda's Kimchi-premium trade (~$1M/day at 30-50% spreads), UST and USDC depeg arbitrage, jaredfromsubway.eth's $22M+ MEV sandwich operation, and large CEX-DEX bots running $2.5M of inventory — were NOT replicable at small size. They required either capital scale, regulatory/banking access (moving fiat across the Korea border), exclusive infrastructure (low-latency colocated nodes, private Flashbots/builder relationships, inventory pre-positioned on both venues), or simply being predatory toward retail. Notably, a forensic breakdown of one $2.5M-capital CEX-DEX bot showed a single real trade netted ~$0.45 (and could have been a $0.20 LOSS) — the edge is volume and inventory management, not per-trade margin. (2) The honest middle: a documented 3-month DIY flash-loan/DEX arbitrage bot ("FlashArb") earned ~$24.6k net ($8.2k/mo) but only AFTER 71.5% success rate, $8.4k burned on reverted txs, 15% still front-run, and only 0.006% of 2.4M scanned opportunities being viable — i.e. real money but a brutal arms race. For a small HIVE/MELEK-funded bot the realistic, replicable edge is NOT atomic MEV or millisecond CEX races. It is: persistent fee-cleared spreads on thin/illiquid pairs and IOU/token internal markets (wider gaps, less competition), listing/announcement lag (a token spikes on one venue and lags minutes elsewhere), and slow stablecoin/IOU depegs that last hours-to-days (UST stayed below peg for days; USDC sat at $0.87-0.99 for ~3 days) — windows long enough to act on without colocation. Every spread must be netted against BOTH trading fees, withdrawal/network fees, slippage on thin books, and execution risk (one leg not filling, exchange halts, withdrawal freezes). Practitioners cite ~$20k-50k/trade as the minimum for cross-exchange spot arb to clear fees — so the small bot's realistic home is internal/on-chain markets where there is no withdrawal step, and patient depeg/IOU mispricing, not cross-CEX latency racing.

cases.name: SBF / Alameda Kimchi Premium (South Korea, 2017-2020)
cases.what: Bitcoin and other crypto traded persistently 30-50% (sometimes up to 80%) higher on South Korean exchanges than US/global venues. Alameda reportedly cleared up to ~$1M/day at peak; e.g. BTC ~$10k US vs ~$15k Korea.
cases.approxProfit: Up to ~$1,000,000/day at peak; spreads of 30-50%, occasionally up to 80%.
cases.howItWorked: Buy BTC cheap on US/global exchange, move it to a Korean exchange, sell at the premium, then convert KRW proceeds back to USD and repatriate. The hard part was NOT the trade but the fiat plumbing: Korean capital controls and banking limits made repatriating KRW and cycling capital back the binding constraint. Alameda solved the banking/forex side at scale, which is why it captured the edge while domestic Koreans (blocked by capital controls) and most foreigners could not.

cases.name: UST (TerraUSD) Depeg Arbitrage (May 2022)
cases.what: Algorithmic stablecoin UST broke its $1 peg starting May 7-10, 2022, trading as low as ~$0.985 then collapsing far below. The protocol let anyone burn $1-of-UST for $1-of-LUNA, so sub-peg UST was a redemption arb.
cases.approxProfit: Roughly 1 cent per token at the early shallow depeg (buy UST at $0.99, redeem for $1 of LUNA); much larger nominal gaps as it collapsed, but capped by mint capacity and crashing LUNA price.
cases.howItWorked: Buy UST below $1 on the open market, burn it via Terra's mint/redeem for $1 worth of freshly minted LUNA, sell the LUNA. The catch: the protocol capped UST burns at $100M/day, so arbitrage could not absorb the panic; the redemption flood hyperinflated LUNA supply (343M to 6.53 trillion in a week), so most arbitrageurs were selling into a collapsing asset — profitable only with fast execution and small early size, ruinous late.

cases.name: USDC Depeg During SVB Collapse (March 2023)
cases.what: Circle disclosed $3.3B of USDC reserves stuck at failed Silicon Valley Bank; USDC fell to a low of $0.8726 on Mar 11, sat at $0.87-0.99, and re-pegged to $1 by Mar 13 once the FDIC backstopped SVB deposits.
cases.approxProfit: Buying near $0.88-0.90 and holding to the $1.00 re-peg = roughly 10-13% over ~2-3 days; DEX volume spiked 249% ($7.14B to $25.0B) as flows ran through MakerDAO PSM and DEXes.
cases.howItWorked: A convergence/recovery trade, not atomic arb: buy discounted USDC (or swap depegged USDC->DAI via MakerDAO's Peg Stability Module 1:1) on the bet that a fully-collateralized fiat stablecoin with a solvent issuer would re-peg once the banking question resolved. The PSM also acted as an exit ramp, which dragged correlated stables (USDP, GUSD) down. The edge was a multi-DAY window and a fundamental thesis on backing — slow enough for a non-HFT trader, but carrying genuine 'it never re-pegs' tail risk (the lesson UST taught the week before).

cases.name: jaredfromsubway.eth MEV Sandwich Bot (2023-2026)
cases.what: The most notorious Ethereum MEV bot; sandwiches victim swaps on Uniswap/SushiSwap by front-running and back-running them. Documented sandwiching even Vitalik Buterin's swap (May 2026) using ~$1.14M WETH to move price; runs multi-layer (5- and 7-victim) sandwiches.
cases.approxProfit: ~$22M total since March 2023 per EigenPhi (June 2024); earlier estimates ~$34M; one disputed estimate ~$3.5-4.5M proceeds. ~765 ETH (~$2M) over 85,000 txs on one address by Aug 2024.
cases.howItWorked: Monitor the mempool for large pending AMM swaps, buy the token just before the victim (front-run, pushing price up), let the victim execute at the worse price, then sell immediately after (back-run) capturing the spread the victim's trade created. Requires extremely high gas bidding, mempool access, and contract optimization; profits come FROM retail traders' slippage. Not arbitrage of a real price gap — value extraction.

cases.name: $2.5M-Capital CEX-DEX Arbitrage Bot (forensic breakdown)
cases.what: Public reverse-engineering of an on-chain bot running ~$2.5M inventory on a single ETH wallet. It bought USUAL cheap on Binance while selling on Uniswap (or vice-versa) when an on-chain price move opened a gap.
cases.approxProfit: ~$0.45 USDT on the analyzed single trade — and the author notes it could have been a ~$0.20 LOSS under slightly different fee assumptions. Profit is in VOLUME across thousands of such trades, not per-trade margin.
cases.howItWorked: Detect an on-chain price-moving tx (mempool/block), execute the DEX leg (sold 24,095 USUAL for 0.6643 ETH, ~$2.11 gas) and the offsetting CEX legs on Binance (buy 24,095 USUAL, sell the ETH), netting the tiny CEX-vs-DEX spread minus ~$0.49 Binance taker fees and gas. Edge = pre-positioned inventory on BOTH sides (no slow withdrawal between legs), fast signal detection, possible builder ties, and razor-thin fees at scale. The author calls the 2.39s reaction 'really slow' — frontier teams are faster.

cases.name: FlashArb DIY Flash-Loan DEX Arbitrage Bot (3-month production run)
cases.type: DEX/AMM atomic arbitrage via flash loans (DIY)
cases.what: A developer's honest 3-month production post-mortem running a flash-loan-funded atomic DEX arbitrage bot on Ethereum (multi-pool price-discrepancy cycles, submitted as private Flashbots bundles).
cases.approxProfit: Gross $47,320; net ~$24,640 over 3 months (~$8,213/mo) after $12,180 gas on wins, $8,400 gas on reverts, $2,100 infra. 892 of 1,247 submitted txs succeeded (71.5%); only 0.006% of 2.4M scanned opportunities were viable; ~15% still front-run.
cases.howItWorked: Scan many DEX pools for a price-discrepancy cycle (e.g. same token cheaper on Curve than Balancer), borrow the capital via a flash loan, execute all legs in ONE atomic transaction (revert-if-unprofitable, so no inventory/hedging risk), and submit as a private Flashbots bundle to dodge public-mempool front-running. Gas efficiency was the edge (180-220k gas/tx vs competitors' 350-500k). Author explicitly calls it 'a race to the bottom' and warns most such bots fail. Real money, but needs a node, contract dev skill, infra, and tolerance for thousands in burned gas.

cases.name: New-Listing / Announcement Price-Lag Arbitrage
cases.what: When a major exchange (e.g. Coinbase/Binance) lists or announces a token, its price spikes there while lagging on smaller venues (KuCoin, Gate.io) for seconds-to-minutes; new-exchange listings can lag established price discovery for hours.
cases.approxProfit: Variable; gap is the listing pop minus fees. Cross-CEX BTC example cited ~$250/BTC on a ~0.33% gap. On thin/new tokens the gap can be several percent for minutes.
cases.howItWorked: Pre-fund accounts on multiple exchanges with USDT/USDC so no slow transfer is needed mid-trade; on a listing/announcement, buy where the token is still cheap and sell where it spiked, settling the gap before others close it. Hours-long lag on new-exchange listings is the most accessible variant. Binding constraints: speed (windows are seconds-minutes), and the withdrawal-delay trap if funds aren't already on both venues — moving tokens between chains/CEXes takes time that kills the gap.

cases.name: Triangular Arbitrage on a Single Exchange (e.g. Binance)
cases.what: Cycle three pairs (e.g. USDT->BTC->ETH->USDT) when the implied cross-rate diverges from the direct rate within one exchange. Academic study found 4,879 opportunities on Binance BTC/LTC/USD high-frequency data.
cases.approxProfit: Per-cycle gaps are tiny (basis points). One illustrative buy-buy-sell example cited 2,000 USDT, but realistic net edges are fractions of a percent and mostly eaten by the 3x taker fees.
cases.howItWorked: Compute whether trading A->B->C->A leaves more A than you started with after all three fees. No withdrawal step (all on one exchange) is the attractive part for a small operator. But: Binance has no batch trading, so all three legs must fire near-simultaneously with timing/leg-fill risk; you compete with HFT bots; and three taker fees usually exceed the gap. Study conclusion: opportunities exist but transaction costs and capacity make them largely non-exploitable for retail.

cases.name: Cross-Chain Bridge Arbitrage (same asset, different chains)
cases.what: The same token trades at different prices on different chains (e.g. a stablecoin pumped by a BSC yield farm vs its flat Polygon price); buy on the cheap chain, bridge, sell on the expensive chain.
cases.approxProfit: Only profitable on large gaps or large size; a 0.5% gap commonly nets -0.2% after ~0.4% fees + ~0.2% slippage + bridge/gas.
cases.howItWorked: Identify a cross-chain price gap, bridge funds, sell on the high side. The structural problem for a small bot: bridge latency (minutes to much longer) is directional-risk exposure, gaps close while you're bridging, and small discrepancies need large size to clear fixed bridge+gas costs. Research notes a sophisticated minority dominates this due to pre-distributed inventory across chains and low-latency infra.

patterns: Net, don't gross: every spread must clear BOTH sides' trading fees + withdrawal/network/gas fees + slippage on thin books + execution risk. Practitioners cite ~$20k-50k/trade as the minimum for cross-CEX spot arb to even clear fees — a 0.5% gross gap is routinely -0.2% net. Wire a hard 'net-of-all-costs > threshold' gate into the brain before any signal becomes a trade.

The small-bot's real edge is TIME, not SPEED. Atomic MEV and cross-CEX races are won in milliseconds by colocated teams with builder relationships and pre-positioned inventory — not replicable for us. Patient, slow-moving mispricings (multi-day stablecoin/IOU depegs like USDC's ~3-day $0.87->$1.00, hours-long new-exchange listing lag) are windows long enough for a modest bot to act on.

Thin/illiquid pairs and internal/IOU token markets have wider, more persistent, less-contested spreads than BTC/ETH on major venues. This is the documented home turf for retail — but illiquid coins also move violently, so size small and treat the wide spread as compensation for fill risk, not free money. (Directly relevant to MELEK/HIVE-Engine internal markets and IOU books where there is NO withdrawal leg.)

Eliminate the withdrawal/bridge leg whenever possible. The recurring profit-killer across every CEX-CEX and cross-chain case is the transfer time between venues: gaps close while funds are in transit, and funds can be frozen by KYC/AML/maintenance. Prefer single-venue internal markets (one exchange's triangular cycles, on-chain DEX atomic swaps, HIVE/MELEK internal order books) where settlement is instant and there is no withdrawal-delay trap.

Pre-fund both sides in advance with stable assets so you never move capital mid-trade. The fastest practical cross-venue arb keeps balances parked on every venue and only rebalances occasionally — converting the trade into two simultaneous opposite orders rather than a buy-then-transfer-then-sell.

Depeg/convergence trades carry a real tail: 'it never re-pegs.' USDC re-pegged (solvent issuer + FDIC backstop) the same week UST went to zero (algorithmic, no real backing). Only take depeg-recovery trades where the asset has genuine, verifiable collateral and a credible re-peg mechanism; size to survive being wrong.

Most scanned 'opportunities' are fake or already gone. The FlashArb data (0.006% of 2.4M opportunities viable; 28.5% of submitted txs reverted; 15% front-run) shows the dominant cost is acting on stale/illusory gaps. Validate against live order-book depth and recent fills before committing; budget for losing trades and reverts as a normal line item, not a bug. (Mirrors our own task #23 fix: drop arb signals with legs too far off spot.)

Reaction speed and data freshness gate everything. Delayed or inconsistent price data makes a bot trade gaps that no longer exist — the single most common retail loss. For a slow bot this means deliberately targeting only spreads wide enough and persistent enough to survive our latency, and rejecting anything in the sub-second/HFT regime.

Sandwich/predatory MEV (jaredfromsubway-style) is a documented multi-million-dollar business but it profits FROM retail slippage, not from real arbitrage — out of scope ethically and technically (needs gas-war infra). Worth knowing as a threat model: our own DEX swaps can be sandwiched, so route through private/Flashbots-style bundles or set tight slippage when we transact on AMMs.

Profit at small size comes from many small, boring, repeatable net-positive trades — not one heroic spread. The honest cases that a modest operator can touch (USDC re-peg, listing lag, thin internal-market spreads) are low-frequency and low-margin; the brain should treat arb as a steady trickle to harvest opportunistically, not a primary revenue engine, and never lever up to chase it.
